{{Short description|Special case of the polylogarithm}}
{{redirect|Li2|the molecule with formula Li<sub>2</sub>|dilithium}}
{{See also|polylogarithm#Dilogarithm}}
[[Image:Mplwp dilogarithm.svg|thumb|right|325px|The dilogarithm along the real axis]]
[[File:Complex polylog2.jpg|thumb|right|325px|The [[principal value]] of the dilogarithm plotted in the complex plane]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''dilogarithm''' (or '''Spence's function'''), denoted as {{math|Li<sub>2</sub>(''z'')}}, is a particular case of the [[polylogarithm]]. Two related [[special functions]] are referred to as Spence's function, the dilogarithm itself:
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(z) = -\int_0^z{\ln(1-u) \over u}\, du \text{, }z \in \Complex</math> 
and its reflection.
For {{math|{{abs|''z''}} ≤ 1}}, an [[infinite series]] also applies (the integral definition constitutes its analytical extension to the [[complex plane]]):
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(z) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty {z^k \over k^2}.</math>

Alternatively, the dilogarithm function is sometimes defined as 
:<math>\int_{1}^{v} \frac{ \ln t }{ 1 -t } dt = \operatorname{Li}_2(1-v).</math>

In [[hyperbolic geometry]] the dilogarithm can be used to compute the volume of an [[ideal simplex]]. Specifically, a simplex whose vertices have [[cross ratio]] {{mvar|z}} has [[hyperbolic volume]]
:<math>D(z) = \operatorname{Im} \operatorname{Li}_2(z) + \arg(1-z) \log|z|.</math>
The function {{math|''D''(''z'')}} is sometimes called the Bloch-Wigner function.<ref>Zagier p. 10</ref> [[Lobachevsky's function]] and [[Clausen's function]] are closely related functions.

[[William Spence (mathematician)|William Spence]], after whom the function was named by early writers in the field, was a Scottish mathematician working in the early nineteenth century.<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Spence/|title = William Spence - Biography}}</ref> He was at school with [[John Galt (novelist)|John Galt]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.biographi.ca/009004-119.01-e.php?BioId=37522|title = Biography – GALT, JOHN – Volume VII (1836-1850) – Dictionary of Canadian Biography}}</ref> who later wrote a biographical essay on Spence.

==Analytic structure==
Using the former definition above, the dilogarithm function is analytic everywhere on the complex plane except at <math>z = 1</math>, where it has a logarithmic branch point. The standard choice of branch cut is along the positive real axis <math>(1, \infty)</math>. However, the function is continuous at the branch point and takes on the value <math>\operatorname{Li}_2(1) = \pi^2/6</math>.

==Identities==
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(z)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-z)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Li}_2(z^2).</math><ref name="Zagier">Zagier</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(1-z)+\operatorname{Li}_2\left(1-\frac{1}{z}\right)=-\frac{(\ln z)^2}{2}.</math><ref name="MathWorld">{{MathWorld|title=Dilogarithm|urlname=Dilogarithm}}</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(z)+\operatorname{Li}_2(1-z)=\frac{{\pi}^2}{6}-\ln z \cdot\ln(1-z).</math><ref name="Zagier"/> The [[reflection formula]].
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(-z)-\operatorname{Li}_2(1-z)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Li}_2(1-z^2)=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{12}-\ln z \cdot \ln(z+1).</math><ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(z) +\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{z}\right) = - \frac{\pi^2}{6} - \frac{(\ln(-z))^2}{2}.</math><ref name="Zagier"/>
:<math>\operatorname{L}(x)+\operatorname{L}(y)=\operatorname{L}(xy)+\operatorname{L}\left(\frac{x(1-y)}{1-xy}\right)+\operatorname{L}\left(\frac{y(1-x)}{1-xy}\right)</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Rogers L-Function |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rogers |first=L. J. |date=1907 |title=On the Representation of Certain Asymptotic Series as Convergent Continued Fractions |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/plms/s2-4.1.72 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s2-4 |issue=1 |pages=72–89 |doi=10.1112/plms/s2-4.1.72|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Abel's functional equation or five-term relation where <math>\operatorname{L}(z)=\frac{\pi^2}{6}[\operatorname{Li}_2(z)+\frac12\ln(z)\ln(1-z)]</math> is the [[Leonard James Rogers|Rogers]] [[L-function]] (an analogous relation is satisfied also by the [[quantum dilogarithm]])

==Particular value identities==
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=\frac{{\pi}^2}{18}-\frac{(\ln 3)^2}{6}.</math><ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{18}+\frac{(\ln 3)^2}{6}.</math><ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{18}+\ln2\cdot \ln3-\frac{(\ln 2)^2}{2}-\frac{(\ln 3)^2}{3}.</math><ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=\frac{{\pi}^2}{18}+2\ln2\cdot\ln3-2(\ln 2)^2-\frac{2}{3}(\ln 3)^2.</math> <ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right)+\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\ln{\frac{9}{8}}\right)^2.</math><ref name="MathWorld"/>
:<math>36\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-36\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-12\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+6\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{64}\right)={\pi}^2.</math>

==Special values==
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(-1)=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{12}.</math>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(0)=0.</math> Its slope = 1.
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{{\pi}^2}{12}-\frac{(\ln 2)^2}{2}.</math>
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(1) = \zeta(2) = \frac{{\pi}^2}{6},</math> where <math>\zeta(s)</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]].
:<math>\operatorname{Li}_2(2)=\frac{{\pi}^2}{4}-i\pi\ln2.</math>
:<math>\begin{align}
\operatorname{Li}_2\left(-\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\right)
&=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{15}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\ln\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}\right)^2 \\
&=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{15}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}^2 2.
\end{align}</math>
:<math>\begin{align}
\operatorname{Li}_2\left(-\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}\right)
&=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{10}-\ln^2 \frac{\sqrt5+1}{2} \\
&=-\frac{{\pi}^2}{10}-\operatorname{arcsch}^2 2.
\end{align}</math>
:<math>\begin{align}
\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\right)
&=\frac{{\pi}^2}{15}-\ln^2 \frac{\sqrt5+1}{2} \\
&=\frac{{\pi}^2}{15}-\operatorname{arcsch}^2 2.
\end{align}</math>
:<math>\begin{align}
\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\right)
&=\frac{{\pi}^2}{10}-\ln^2 \frac{\sqrt5+1}{2} \\
&=\frac{{\pi}^2}{10}-\operatorname{arcsch}^2 2.
\end{align}</math>

==In particle physics==
Spence's Function is commonly encountered in [[particle physics]] while calculating [[Radiative correction|radiative corrections]]. In this context, the function is often defined with an [[absolute value]] inside the logarithm:

:<math>
\operatorname{\Phi}(x) = -\int_0^x \frac{\ln|1-u|}{u} \, du = 
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Li}_2(x), & x \leq 1; \\ \frac{\pi^2}{3} - \frac{1}{2}(\ln x)^2 - \operatorname{Li}_2(\frac{1}{x}), & x > 1.
\end{cases}
</math>
